t76a_losh1.headline: AI Generated
flagged: AI-Generated (134 words): Then there are the things that are hardest to tell anyone, even though they're often what you most need help with, like an urge that scares you or something you did that could get you in legal trouble. Before you tell, know where it can end up. Anything you write online or in an AI app can be screenshotted, or kept and handed over when a court asks for it, and a fake name or a deleted message won't make you anonymous. Therapists, doctors, teachers and some others may have to report certain things, and a few rules apply to everyone, depending on where you live. That doesn't mean every crime you mention gets reported, though. The police aren't there to keep your secrets the way a therapist might, either.

t76a_ue2.headline: AI Generated
flagged: AI-Generated (168 words): Physical pain can set off that urge too, and then the escape plan might be whatever numbed it last time, even if you know it makes things worse. When the pain gets unbearable, taking care of yourself can mean calling urgent medical services to get it looked at, and maybe treated, even if earlier tests never found the cause. Normal results don't make your pain imaginary. If severe pain keeps coming back, though, I wouldn't make the emergency room the plan for every attack. Ask your doctor about a pain specialist and a written plan for the flare-ups you can see coming, with urgent care as the backup. In France, for example, a doctor can request an assessment at a chronic pain center, and ask for priority when it's warranted, but nothing guarantees you an appointment or a particular medicine. And if the pain has you thinking about dying, the first steps in If You Want to Kill Yourself come before all of this.
